items.tldr: In AI/LLM contexts, a harness is the scaffolding code that runs a model against tasks or evals — handling prompting, tool calls, parsing, and scoring.
Reducing the numerical precision of an LLM's weights (e.g., from 16-bit to 4-bit) to shrink memory footprint and speed up inference, usually with minor accuracy loss.
Specialized hardware (GPUs, TPUs, NPUs, or custom ASICs like Groq or Cerebras chips) designed to speed up AI workloads such as training and inference beyond what general-purpose CPUs can deliver.
A quick eval prompt designed to detect "slop" — generic, low-quality LLM output patterns — by probing a model's skill on tasks where slop typically surfaces.
Large Language Model — a neural network trained on massive text corpora to predict and generate language, powering chatbots, agents, and most modern AI tooling.
GGUF is a binary file format for storing quantized LLM weights and metadata, designed for fast loading and inference with llama.cpp and compatible runtimes.
Text-based User Interface — a terminal-rendered interactive UI, commonly used for AI dev tools like Claude Code, Aider, and other CLI agent harnesses.
Open-source memory library (with managed service) by Plastic Labs for building stateful LLM agents that model users and other entities continually across sessions.

Router-weighted Expert Activation Pruning — a one-shot MoE compression method that prunes redundant experts using router gate-values and expert activation norms while preserving the router's control over remaining experts.
A personal knowledge management system—often a note database like Obsidian or Notion augmented with LLMs and RAG—that stores and retrieves your notes, ideas, and references on demand.

EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) is a security platform category where LLMs are increasingly used to auto-generate detection rules against proprietary EDR schemas, requiring normalization layers to mitigate hallucinations.

A neural network architecture where multiple specialized sub-networks (experts) exist, and a gating mechanism routes each input to only a few experts, enabling large parameter counts with efficient inference.
Distillation is the process of training a smaller "student" model to mimic the outputs of a larger "teacher" model, transferring capabilities while reducing size and inference cost.
AI models whose trained parameters are publicly released, allowing anyone to run, fine-tune, or distill them locally, though training data and code may remain closed.
In transformer LLM inference, a memory store of previously computed key and value tensors from attention layers, reused across tokens to avoid recomputing them and dramatically speed up generation.
LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) fine-tunes LLMs by training small adapter matrices instead of full weights; QLoRA does the same on top of a quantized base model to slash memory usage.
A technique that augments an LLM's responses by first retrieving relevant documents or context from an external knowledge base and injecting them into the prompt.
vLLM is a high-throughput, memory-efficient inference and serving engine for LLMs, best known for PagedAttention which optimizes KV cache management to boost throughput.
An open-source C/C++ library for running LLM inference locally on CPUs and GPUs, popularized by its efficient support for quantized GGUF models on consumer hardware.

SGLang is a fast-serving engine for LLMs and vision language models that co-designs the backend runtime and frontend language , using RadixAttention for prefix caching to compete with vLLM and TensorRT-LLM.

Optimized quantization and inference library for running LLMs locally on consumer NVIDIA GPUs, using the EXL3 format (a streamlined QTIP variant) with tensor parallelism, speculative decoding, and cache quantization.
LM Studio is a desktop application for discovering, downloading, and running local LLMs (typically GGUF models via llama.cpp) with a chat UI and OpenAI-compatible API server.
A throughput metric measuring how many tokens an LLM generates (or processes) per second, commonly used to benchmark inference speed across models, hardware, and serving frameworks.
NVIDIA's compact desktop "personal AI supercomputer" powered by the GB10 Grace Blackwell Superchip with 128GB unified memory, capable of running local models up to ~200B parameters.
The maximum number of tokens an LLM can process at once as input, including the prompt, conversation history, and retrieved context, before older content must be truncated.

NVIDIA's hardware-native 4-bit floating-point (E2M1) quantization format for Blackwell GPUs, using 16-element blocks with FP8-E4M3 per-block scales and a per-tensor FP32 scale for efficient LLM inference and training.

Mixed-bit quantization is a technique that assigns different bit-widths to different weights or layers of a model, preserving accuracy on sensitive components while aggressively compressing less critical ones.

Bittensor is a decentralized peer-to-peer network organized into task-specific subnets (language modeling, inference, image generation, etc.) where miners and validators contribute AI services and earn the native TAO token.

Decentralized training is the practice of training large AI models across geographically distributed, often heterogeneous compute nodes rather than in a single centralized data center, coordinating gradients or model updates over the network.
MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard from Anthropic that lets LLMs connect to external tools, data sources, and services through a unified client-server interface.
Self-custody means holding your own private keys (or model weights, data, or agent credentials) directly rather than trusting a third-party service to store them for you.
Maximal Extractable Value — profit validators or searchers extract by reordering, inserting, or censoring transactions in a block, increasingly relevant when AI agents transact on-chain.
A feature in Git that lets you check out multiple branches simultaneously in separate directories, commonly used by AI coding agents to run parallel tasks without conflicts.

oMLX is a macOS-native LLM inference server built on Apple's MLX framework using zero-copy unified memory and a two-tier KV cache (unified memory + SSD) for high token generation speeds on Apple Silicon.
Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback: a training technique where human preferences are used to fine-tune an LLM's outputs, typically via a reward model guiding policy optimization.
LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that trains small low-rank matrices added to a frozen base model instead of updating all its weights.
